Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Labial trauma

A two-patient uncontrolled report describes improved healing and pain after treatment. It does not establish a causal effect or applicability to routine lip injuries.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A two-patient uncontrolled report describes improved healing and pain after treatment. It does not establish a causal effect or applicability to routine lip injuries.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Oral > Labial trauma/injury category contains one human case series involving two patients with spastic cerebral palsy; no controlled study is listed.

Human and clinical evidence

Low-intensity laser treatment was followed by faster soft-tissue healing, less secondary contamination and analgesia over 14 days. The uncontrolled two-case design cannot establish a causal effect (Moreira et al. 2004). Both patients had spastic cerebral palsy, so repeated lip trauma, motor impairment, oral care, and baseline healing may differ from uncomplicated accidental lip injury. The report describes clinical course rather than standardized wound measurements, blinded assessment, or a prespecified comparator. It cannot determine whether benefit came from analgesia, reduced inflammation, changes in local care, or natural healing. No data address lacerations requiring sutures, infection prevention, scarring, recurrence of self-injury, dose-response, or uncommon harms. This is therefore hypothesis-generating evidence for adjunctive care in a highly selected setting, not evidence for routine management of labial trauma.

Primary original study: Moreira et al. 2004

Animal evidence

none identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

none identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The report describes a 685 nm red diode laser and repeated applications, with treatment on two days, a one-week pause, and two further treatment days. 685 nm is visible red. The exposure regimen is reported for recurrent trauma in patients with spastic cerebral palsy and should not be generalized to other wounds.

Interpretation

The report is hypothesis-generating for a selected population with recurring injury. Motor impairment, oral care, and repeated trauma may affect healing independently of light exposure. It does not establish efficacy for lacerations requiring sutures, prevention of infection or scarring, or a standard dose.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low. One uncontrolled two-patient series describes improvement.
Publications and records1 unique title.

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The direct evidence is a two-patient case series involving people with spastic cerebral palsy and recurrent traumatic lip injury. Healing and pain improvement were described, but there was no control group, standardized wound assessment, or blinded evaluation. The highly selected context limits conclusions for ordinary accidental labial trauma.
